clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive organic acidaemia caused by deficiency of isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase (IVD), a step in leucine catabolism.
Accumulating isovaleric acid gives a characteristic odour of sweaty feet during acute decompensation, a valuable bedside clue.
Presents in two broad patterns: an acute neonatal encephalopathic crisis and a chronic intermittent form with recurrent episodes triggered by illness or protein load.
Acute crises feature vomiting, poor feeding, lethargy progressing to coma, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, ketosis and often hyperammonaemia.
Bone-marrow suppression with neutropenia, thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia is common during acute episodes.

Diagnosis is confirmed by the acylcarnitine profile (raised isovalerylcarnitine, C5) and urine organic acids showing isovalerylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid; it is detectable on newborn screening.
Long-term management uses a leucine-restricted diet with glycine and carnitine supplementation to enhance conjugation and excretion of isovaleryl-CoA.
Acute management reverses catabolism with generous energy provision, stops protein transiently and treats intercurrent illness aggressively.
reference.pathophysiology: Isovaleric acidaemia is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in IVD, encoding the mitochondrial flavoenzyme isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, which catalyses the third step in the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acid leucine, converting isovaleryl-CoA to 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA. When the enzyme is deficient, isovaleryl-CoA and its derivatives accumulate upstream of the block. The excess isovaleryl-CoA is hydrolysed to free isovaleric acid, which is directly toxic and responsible for the characteristic odour, and is conjugated with glycine and carnitine to form isovalerylglycine and isovalerylcarnitine that are excreted in urine; these conjugation pathways are the basis of both diagnosis and treatment. Accumulating organic acids and coenzyme-A esters disturb mitochondrial energy metabolism and inhibit other pathways, contributing to high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, secondary hyperammonaemia through interference with ureagenesis, and ketosis. Bone-marrow precursors are sensitive to these metabolites, producing the neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and sometimes pancytopenia seen in acute episodes. Because leucine is derived both from dietary protein and from endogenous protein breakdown, any catabolic stress such as fasting, infection or a protein load accelerates flux through the blocked pathway and can precipitate life-threatening decompensation, particularly in the neonatal period and during intercurrent illness.
additionalDifferentials: Other organic acidaemias (methylmalonic and propionic acidaemia)
Urea cycle disorders presenting with hyperammonaemia
Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (glutaric aciduria type 2)
Neonatal sepsis and other causes of neonatal encephalopathy
Ketotic hypoglycaemia and other causes of high-anion-gap acidosis
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing raised isovalerylcarnitine (C5)
Urine organic acids showing isovalerylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid
Blood gas, anion gap, glucose, ketones, lactate and ammonia during illness
Full blood count to detect neutropenia, thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia
Plasma amino acids and carnitine status
IVD gene sequencing for confirmation and family counselling
Newborn screening result review and confirmatory testing
redFlags: Progressive lethargy, seizures or coma indicating metabolic encephalopathy
Severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis unresponsive to initial resuscitation
Neutropenic sepsis or severe cytopenias during an acute crisis
Signs of cerebral oedema or raised intracranial pressure
reference.prognosis: With newborn screening, prompt treatment of crises and a leucine-restricted diet with glycine and carnitine, many patients achieve normal or near-normal development, though severe neonatal crises can be fatal or leave neurological sequelae.
pitfalls: Attributing a neonatal presentation to sepsis alone and missing the underlying metabolic disorder
Continuing normal protein intake or allowing fasting during acute illness, worsening decompensation
Overlooking the characteristic odour as a diagnostic clue
Misreading the acute cytopenias as primary haematological or infective disease
Under-treating intercurrent illnesses that can rapidly precipitate a crisis
references: Newborn screening and metabolic medicine guidelines
management: Lifelong leucine (protein) restriction with a specialised metabolic formula to limit isovaleryl-CoA accumulation
Glycine and L-carnitine supplementation to conjugate isovaleric acid into non-toxic, readily excreted products
Emergency sick-day regimen during intercurrent illness: temporary withdrawal of natural protein with high-energy intake and intravenous glucose to reverse catabolism
Acute crisis management with fluids and glucose, correction of high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and ammonia-lowering measures, escalating to haemodialysis for severe hyperammonaemia
Monitoring of growth and development, acylcarnitine profile, ammonia and full blood count for neutropenia and thrombocytopenia
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with sibling and family screening, aided by newborn screening detection
Involvement of a metabolic dietitian and specialist metabolic team for coordinated long-term care
